question: A search algorithm checks the middle door of a sorted row of lockers. If the target is smaller, it says 'search the left half'; if larger, 'search the right half'. Even though the algorithm calls itself, why doesn't it run forever? || a) The compiler automatically limits how many times a function may call itself. | b) The middle door is always checked twice, which guarantees the number is found. | c) Each call is handed a smaller problem, about half as many doors, so it eventually reaches a case that answers immediately. | d) Recursive calls run in parallel, so all halves are searched at once and finish together.
key: c
review_note: Tests recursion termination, as the window frames it.

question: A classmate writes a recursive search over a sorted array of exam scores. It returns false if the range is empty and returns true if the middle score matches. But when the target is less than the middle score, it calls search on the entire original array again instead of the left half. Explain what goes wrong, and describe how to fix it so the function both terminates and correctly finds scores.
key: Calling search on the entire array hands the function the same-sized problem each time, so it never makes progress and recurses forever, or until it runs out of memory. Its base cases, an empty range or a matching middle, are never reached for targets smaller than the middle. The fix is to recurse only on the left half, the elements before the middle, when the target is smaller, and only on the right half when it is larger. Each call then works on about half as many elements, so it eventually hits a base case: the score is found or the range is empty.
verifier_answer: Calling search on the entire original array can repeat the same middle comparison indefinitely: the problem does not shrink, so neither base case is reached. Keep the empty-range and matching-middle base cases. If the target is smaller, recursively search only the current range to the left of the middle; if larger, search only the range to the right. Exclude the middle element in both cases. Each call then strictly shrinks the range while preserving the only region where the target could occur, eventually returning true for a match or false for an empty range.

question: A function checks an array of n numbers for duplicates. For every i from 0 to n−1, and for every j from 0 to n−1 with j ≠ i, it compares numbers[i] with numbers[j] and sets a flag if they are equal. It never stops early. Its exact step count is about 3n² + 2n + 5. Give its big O, omega and theta running times, and justify each.
key: Big O: O(n²). The nested loops produce about n² comparisons, and when we drop the constant 3 and the lower-order terms 2n and 5, n² dominates. Omega: Ω(n²). The function never stops early, so even a best-case input, such as one with a duplicate at the very start, still runs every iteration. Theta: Θ(n²). The upper and lower bounds are the same, so theta applies. Each comparison takes constant time, so the nested loops alone determine the growth.
verifier_answer: O(n²), Ω(n²), and Θ(n²). The dominant term in 3n² + 2n + 5 is n²; constants and lower-order terms do not affect asymptotic growth. Because both loops run fully regardless of the values, best- and worst-case work are quadratic, giving matching upper and lower bounds and therefore a tight Θ(n²) bound.

question: [0] Selection sort keeps track of only the smallest element seen so far in a single variable, rather than memorizing every value. [1] Because of this, it rediscovers the next smallest element on each pass, even though it has already looked at every number before. [2] This is an example of a trade-off between memory and running time. [3] Since the comparisons total n(n−1)/2, we keep only the dominant n² term and say selection sort is in O(n²).
key: correct
review_note: Correct scenario; every sentence checks out.

question: [0] Plain bubble sort makes all of its comparisons even on an already sorted list, so it is O(n²) in the worst case. [1] We can improve it by stopping after any pass of the inner loop that makes no swaps. [2] With this change, a sorted list needs just one pass, so the best case is Ω(n). [3] Since the lower bound is now n, the improved bubble sort runs in Θ(n) overall.
key: flawed:3 — The best case is Ω(n), but the average and worst cases remain on the order of n². Because the big O and Omega bounds differ, we cannot state a single Θ for bubble sort.
review_note: Sentence 0 ties "sorted list" to the worst case awkwardly, but is true.

question: [0] A recursive function is a function that calls itself somewhere in its own body. [1] For the Mario pyramid, a pyramid of height n can be defined as a pyramid of height n - 1 plus one more row. [2] As long as the function has a base case, it does not matter whether the recursive call passes n or n - 1, because the base case will eventually stop it. [3] A base case like if (n <= 0) return; answers immediately without calling the function again.
key: flawed:2 — Each recursive call must pass a smaller problem, such as n - 1, so the input shrinks toward the base case. If draw(n) called draw(n), it would never reach n <= 0 and would recurse forever.

question: [0] Merge sort works by sorting the left half, sorting the right half, and then merging the two sorted halves. [1] Its base case is a list of one element, which is already sorted, so there is nothing to do. [2] To merge, you point at the front of each sorted half and repeatedly move the smaller number to the output. [3] After placing each number, both pointers go back to the start of their halves so that no smaller number is missed. [4] Repeated halving of 8 numbers gives 3 levels, and each level involves merging all 8 numbers.
key: flawed:3 — After taking the smaller number, only that half's pointer moves one step to the right. Neither pointer ever resets, so each number is examined once and merging takes about n steps.

question: A program has already done t = malloc(strlen(s) + 1); and now wants to copy the string s into t using the standard library instead of a loop. Which call is correct, and what happens to s if the program then capitalizes t[0]? || a) strcpy(s, t); s is also capitalized because both refer to the same characters | b) strcpy(s, t); s stays unchanged because t has its own memory | c) strcpy(t, s); s is also capitalized because both refer to the same characters | d) strcpy(t, s); s stays unchanged because t has its own memory
key: d

question: A programmer wants space for 3 integers and writes int *x = malloc(3 * sizeof(int)); instead of int *x = malloc(12);. Why is the sizeof version preferred? || a) malloc's argument is a count of integers, so sizeof converts it into bytes for the compiler. | b) sizeof makes malloc initialize every integer to 0. | c) An int is not 4 bytes on every system, so asking for sizeof(int) keeps the code correct and portable. | d) Using sizeof guarantees malloc will never return NULL.
key: c

question: A program calls int *x = malloc(3 * sizeof(int)); on line 8, stores three values using indices 0, 1 and 2, and then returns from main without ever calling free(x). On a system where an int is 4 bytes, what is Valgrind's leak summary most likely to report? || a) Invalid write of size 4 at line 8 | b) Definitely lost 12 bytes in 1 block, traced back to the allocation on line 8 | c) All heap blocks were freed, no leaks are possible, because the operating system reclaims memory when the program exits | d) Definitely lost 4 bytes in 3 blocks, traced back to the last line of main
key: b
review_note: Revised after PR review: now a leak, not an invalid write.

question: Consider this code: int *x; int *y; x = malloc(sizeof(int)); *x = 42; *y = 13;. Which statement is the dangerous one? || a) int *x; because declaring a pointer without an equal sign is illegal | b) x = malloc(sizeof(int)); because malloc can only allocate arrays | c) *x = 42; because x has not been given a pointee | d) *y = 13; because y was never set to point anywhere
key: d

question: A student writes int *count; *count = 0; at the start of main, intending to use count as a counter that other code updates through the pointer. Explain what is wrong with this code and describe two different ways to fix it so that *count = 0 becomes safe.
key: Declaring int *count only creates the pointer. It does not give count a pointee, so count holds a garbage address. The statement *count = 0 goes to that random address and tries to store 0 there, which can crash the program or corrupt memory. The first fix is to allocate a pointee: write count = malloc(sizeof(int));, check that count is not NULL, then do *count = 0;, and later call free(count). The second fix is to point count at an existing variable: declare int n; and assign count = &n;. Then *count = 0 stores 0 in n.
verifier_answer: Declaring count creates a pointer variable but neither initializes its address nor creates an int pointee. Dereferencing that uninitialized pointer has undefined behavior. Two fixes are: (1) create a local int storage; then set int *count = &storage; before *count = 0;, keeping storage alive while the pointer is used; or (2) use int *count = malloc(sizeof *count);, check count != NULL before *count = 0;, and free(count) when finished.

question: A student writes void add_bonus(int score) { score = score + 10; } and calls add_bonus(grade) in main, where grade is 80. Afterward, main prints 80. Explain why, then rewrite the function header, the body line, and the call so that grade becomes 90.
key: C passes arguments by value, so score is a copy of grade stored in add_bonus's own frame. Adding 10 changes only that copy, and it disappears when the function returns. To fix it, pass by reference: void add_bonus(int *score) { *score = *score + 10; } and call add_bonus(&grade). Now score holds grade's address, and *score goes to that address, so grade itself becomes 90.
verifier_answer: C passes arguments by value, so score is a copy of grade. Changing score leaves grade unchanged. Use the header void add_bonus(int *score), the body line *score = *score + 10;, and the call add_bonus(&grade);. Dereferencing the pointer updates grade itself from 80 to 90.

question: [0] When a program runs, its machine code is copied into RAM and, in the usual picture, sits at the top of memory, with any global variables placed just below it. [1] Below the globals is the heap, the region malloc allocates from, and it grows downward as more memory is requested. [2] At the other end is the stack, which holds local variables and function calls, and it grows upward like trays stacked in a cafeteria. [3] When main calls another function, that function gets its own frame just above main's, and its parameters and local variables live there. [4] If that function calls malloc, the memory it gets back is part of the function's frame, so it is automatically reclaimed when the function returns and never needs to be freed.
key: flawed:4 — Memory from malloc comes from the heap, not the function's stack frame. It stays allocated after the function returns until free is called on its address, and forgetting to free it causes a memory leak.
review_note: Revised: heap vs stack lifetime; directions framed as the picture.

question: [0] Because an array's elements are contiguous, you can use the length to jump straight to the middle element. [1] That makes binary search on a sorted array run in O(log n) time. [2] However, if an array fills up and there's no free space right after it, you must allocate a bigger chunk elsewhere and copy all the old values over. [3] For a few values that's fine, but for millions of values the copying wastes a lot of time.
key: correct

question: [0] A linked list allocates a new node for each value and connects the nodes with pointers, so the nodes can sit wherever free memory happens to be, even if it is fragmented. [1] Because of this, the list can grow and shrink without copying the existing values to a new location, unlike resizing an array with realloc. [2] Searching for a value, deleting a value, and inserting a value into its correct place in a sorted list are all O(n), because you must walk from the head to find the right node, although prepending a node to an unsorted list is O(1). [3] Converting it to a doubly linked list, with pointers in both directions, restores binary search on a sorted list and brings search down to O(log n).
key: flawed:3 — Converting it to a doubly linked list, with pointers in both directions, makes some code easier to write, such as insertion and deletion, but search on a sorted list is still O(n) because finding the middle still requires traversing the nodes one by one.
review_note: Revised: prepend O(1) stated correctly; one flaw only.

question: [0] A binary search tree node stores a number plus a left pointer and a right pointer. [1] Every node is greater than its left child and less than its right child, and this property holds recursively for every subtree. [2] Because the tree grows just by updating pointers, inserting values in any order automatically keeps it balanced, with height about log2 n. [3] When searching, comparing the target with a node lets us ignore an entire subtree, much like tearing a phone book in half.
key: flawed:2 — Insertion order matters. Sorted input makes a naive BST devolve into a linked list with O(n) operations. A logarithmic height is maintained only if the tree is rebalanced on insertion or deletion.

question: A hash table hashes names by their first letter into 26 buckets. A programmer changes it to hash on the first three letters, using one bucket for every combination from AAA to ZZZ. What is the main effect of this change? || a) It eliminates collisions for every possible set of names, at no extra cost | b) It reduces the likelihood of collisions, but it needs vastly more buckets, many of which, like AAA, will sit unused | c) It increases collisions, because three letters are more likely to match than one | d) It shrinks the memory needed, because each bucket's linked list becomes shorter
key: b

question: [0] A hash table is an array of buckets, where each bucket points to the head of a linked list. [1] The hash function turns a key, such as a name, into an index, for example by taking its first letter so that names map to 0 through 25. [2] When two names hash to the same index, the new node is simply chained onto the linked list in that bucket. [3] Because the hash function jumps straight to the right bucket, a hash table lookup always takes O(1) time no matter how many names are stored.
key: flawed:3 — Jumping to the bucket is constant time, but collisions make chains. With k buckets the chains hold about n/k entries, which is still O(n) asymptotically, and the worst case is O(n).

question: Tries achieve effectively constant-time lookup, yet hash tables are used far more often in practice. What is the main trade-off of a trie? || a) Each node holds 26 pointers, most of which are null, so tries use a huge amount of memory | b) Tries cannot store names that are prefixes of other names | c) Trie lookups degrade to O(n) when many names share a first letter | d) Tries must store each full name as a string in every node along its path
key: a
